topic_title: Enforcing a Foreign Arbitral Award in India: A Step-by-Step Guide
angle: A practical guide for a foreign award-holder (or an Indian party resisting enforcement) walking through the Sections 44-49 enforcement route under Part II of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 - what qualifies as a 'foreign award', the documents needed, the narrow grounds of refusal, and how the award converts into an executable decree.
key_points: A 'foreign award' under Section 44 must arise from a commercial relationship, be made in a New York Convention country notified as a reciprocating territory by the Central Government, and be in writing pursuant to an arbitration agreement

Enforcement petition is filed under Sections 47 and 49; the applicant must produce the original (or authenticated copy) award, the original (or certified copy) arbitration agreement, and certified English translations where needed

Section 48 lists the exhaustive, narrow grounds on which an Indian court can refuse enforcement (incapacity, invalid agreement, no proper notice/inability to present case, award beyond scope of submission, improper composition of tribunal, award not yet binding or set aside, subject-matter not arbitrable, or enforcement contrary to Indian public policy) - courts do not re-examine the merits
Once the court is satisfied the award is enforceable under Section 48, it is deemed a decree of the court under Section 49 and can be executed like any Indian civil court decree
Interim relief under Section 9 remains available to protect the award-holder's position even before the award is judicially declared enforceable and attains decree status
India applies a 'commercial reservation' under the New York Convention, so the underlying relationship must qualify as commercial under Indian law for Part II to apply at all
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: Sections 44, 47, 48, 49 framework and the narrow Section 48 refusal grounds: well-settled, confirmed across Bar and Bench, Kluwer Arbitration Blog and multiple practitioner guides at research time

Section 9 interim relief remaining available pre-decree: confirmed via March-April 2026 Bombay High Court coverage and a Supreme Court reference dated 24 April 2026 found at research time - verify the specific case citation when drafting

Exact limitation period for filing an enforcement petition is contested/ambiguous in practitioner commentary (a 'time-bar ambiguity' is flagged by Kluwer) - note this as an open question rather than stating a fixed number of years
India's list of notified reciprocating territories under the New York Convention should be checked against the current official Ministry of Law and Justice notification at drafting time

topic_title: Negotiating a One-Time Settlement (OTS) With Your Bank: What Borrowers Should Know
angle: A practical guide for a borrower whose loan has slipped into NPA, explaining how the RBI's compromise-settlement framework works, what a bank can and cannot offer, and the limits of an OTS - including the point (reinforced by 2026 case law) that a borrower cannot claim OTS as a matter of legal right and that a settlement of the debt does not automatically end related criminal exposure.
key_points: RBI's Framework for Compromise Settlements and Technical Write-offs (June 8, 2023) requires every regulated lender to have a Board-approved OTS policy rather than deciding case-by-case on an ad hoc basis
Loans generally become eligible for OTS consideration once classified as NPA (typically overdue beyond 90 days), when the bank's own recovery-probability assessment drops

Banks are expected to consider the borrower's genuine financial capacity and repayment history in structuring an offer, and courts have held there is no legal entitlement to demand an OTS - it remains the lender's commercial discretion

Practical borrower steps: request the settlement offer in writing on the bank's letterhead, insist on a formal signed Settlement Letter (never rely on a verbal or phone assurance), and confirm the account will be reported as 'settled' (not 'written off' or left ambiguous) to credit bureaus

Settling the outstanding debt through OTS does not by itself terminate independent criminal exposure - if the underlying facts also involve a dishonoured cheque (Section 138 Negotiable Instruments Act) or an allegation of fraud, those proceedings continue separately unless specifically compounded or withdrawn
Banks often intensify NPA resolution drives ahead of financial year-end (October-March), which can be a practical window for borrowers to approach lenders for a settlement discussion
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: RBI Framework for Compromise Settlements and Technical Write-offs dated 8 June 2023 requiring a Board-approved policy: confirmed via multiple 2026 practitioner guides (AMA Legal Solutions, Tulja Legal) at research time

Courts holding OTS is not a matter of legal right for the borrower: consistent with a 2026 High Court ruling already covered on this site ('Writ Dismissed — Borrowers Cannot Claim One Time Settlement as a Matter of Legal Right') - cross-reference that case when drafting rather than restating it as a fresh holding

90-day NPA classification threshold under RBI's IRAC norms: general banking-regulation knowledge, should be cited to the current RBI Master Direction on Income Recognition and Asset Classification at drafting time

Claim that OTS does not end Section 138 or fraud exposure: consistent with general negotiable-instruments and criminal law principle (compounding is a separate step) - verify against current NI Act compounding provisions when drafting

topic_title: Legal Due Diligence Checklist for Buying a Business in India
angle: A practical checklist-style guide for a buyer (or its counsel) preparing to acquire an Indian company or business, covering the core areas of legal due diligence, red flags that commonly derail deals, and how the diligence scope should adapt for cross-border/FDI transactions.
key_points: Core diligence areas: corporate structure and governance (incorporation documents, MOA/AOA, board and shareholder resolutions, statutory registers and MCA filings), share capital and capitalisation table, material contracts, litigation and contingent liabilities, employment and labour compliance, intellectual property ownership, real estate title, regulatory licences and competition/CCI approval requirements, and tax compliance

For cross-border deals, add FEMA and FDI-route compliance to the checklist - sectoral caps, pricing guidelines, and reporting filings (FC-GPR/FC-TRS) need to be verified alongside the general corporate diligence
Data protection compliance (relevant under the DPDP Act) and insurance coverage adequacy are increasingly treated as standalone diligence workstreams rather than folded into 'general contracts'

Diligence is typically conducted through a virtual data room (VDR) where the target uploads corporate records, financials, licences, IP registrations, HR records and compliance certificates for review

Common red flags: unresolved litigation or regulatory show-cause notices, contracts with unassignable change-of-control clauses, lapsed or improperly assigned IP registrations, non-compliant ESOP documentation, and gaps in labour-law registrations (PF/ESI/Shops & Establishment)

Findings typically feed into the transaction documents as specific representations, warranties, indemnities and conditions precedent - diligence is not just an information exercise but shapes deal risk allocation
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: The twelve-area diligence framework (corporate, share capital, contracts, litigation, employment, IP, real estate, regulatory/competition, tax, data protection, financing/security, FEMA/FDI): synthesised from multiple 2026 practitioner checklists (Lexology, Lawsikho, iPleaders) at research time - treat as a general framework, not a statutory list

FC-GPR/FC-TRS reporting requirements under FEMA: well-established RBI/FEMA compliance mechanism - verify current prescribed timelines (typically 30 days) against the current FEMA (Non-Debt Instruments) Rules at drafting time
DPDP Act as a distinct diligence workstream: consistent with this site's own existing DPDP Act compliance guide - cross-reference rather than restate the Act's substantive requirements

topic_title: Are Non-Compete Clauses in Employment Contracts Enforceable in India?
angle: A guide for employers drafting employment contracts and employees evaluating an offer or exit, explaining why post-termination non-compete clauses are generally void under Section 27 of the Indian Contract Act, what remains enforceable during employment, and the narrower tools (confidentiality, non-solicitation, garden leave) employers actually rely on instead.
key_points: Section 27 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 voids any agreement restraining a person from exercising a lawful profession, trade or business - Indian courts have applied this to strike down post-termination non-compete clauses for over a century, with no 'reasonableness' exception unlike UK or US law

Restraints operating during the subsistence of employment (e.g., a bar on moonlighting or working for a competitor while still employed) are generally enforceable, since Section 27 targets restraints that operate after the relationship ends

The main statutory exception is Exception 1 to Section 27, which permits a seller of business goodwill to agree not to carry on a similar business within reasonable local limits - a narrow carve-out that does not extend to ordinary employment

Because outright post-termination non-competes fail, employers in practice rely on non-disclosure/confidentiality clauses (protecting trade secrets and confidential information, which remain enforceable indefinitely), non-solicitation clauses restraining poaching of clients or employees, and garden-leave arrangements during the notice period
Delhi High Court rulings have continued to strike down post-termination non-compete restrictions in employment contracts as unenforceable restraints of trade

Employers should focus contract drafting on precisely defined confidential information and enforceable notice/garden-leave periods rather than broad post-employment competition bans, which Indian courts will not enforce regardless of how the clause is worded
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: Section 27 Indian Contract Act voiding post-termination restraints, with Exception 1 for sale of goodwill: settled, long-established Indian contract law principle, confirmed across multiple practitioner sources at research time

Delhi High Court striking down a post-termination non-compete in 2026: reported by Transatlantic Law International at research time - verify the specific case name and citation when drafting rather than citing it generically

Distinction between during-employment and post-termination restraints: well-settled through Supreme Court precedent (Niranjan Shankar Golikari line of authority) - confirm the lead citation when drafting

topic_title: Captive Power Plant Compliance: The Ownership and Consumption Rules Explained
angle: A practical compliance guide for industrial consumers setting up or investing in a captive generating plant, explaining the twin ownership/consumption test under the Electricity Rules that determines whether the plant qualifies for 'captive' status (and its attendant duty/surcharge benefits), plus the 2026 reform proposals loosening the test.
key_points: To qualify as a 'captive generating plant', a user (or group of users) must meet two tests: own at least 26% of the equity share capital of the generating company, and consume at least 51% of the aggregate electricity generated by the plant on an annual basis

For group captive structures with multiple users, a proportionality formula links the two thresholds (roughly a 1.96 ratio of required consumption percentage to ownership percentage), with a permissible variation band - so a user's required consumption share scales with its shareholding, subject to the 26%/51% floor

Failing either test disqualifies the plant from captive status, exposing the arrangement to cross-subsidy surcharge and other open-access charges that captive consumption is otherwise designed to avoid - a point recently underscored where a hotel was denied captive status for holding only a fraction of the required 26% equity

2026 reform proposals under discussion would shift the consumption test to a collective basis for group captive projects - so long as users together consume 51% of total generation, individual users' shortfalls would no longer disqualify the whole project, easing compliance for multi-user captive structures

Captive status must be certified and is subject to verification by the concerned State Electricity Regulatory Commission or appellate scrutiny at APTEL - documentation of actual annual consumption and shareholding should be maintained contemporaneously, not reconstructed after a dispute arises

This is a live compliance area for industrial groups structuring shared power projects - the ownership stake and offtake commitments in the shareholders' agreement and power purchase arrangement should be drafted to track the regulatory thresholds precisely
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: 26% ownership / 51% consumption twin test under the Electricity Rules, 2005 (as amended): well-established regulatory framework, confirmed across Mercom India, Lexology and law-firm sources at research time
1.96 proportionality ratio and +/-10% variation band: confirmed via Mercom India coverage at research time - verify exact figures against the current text of the Electricity Rules at drafting time

2026 draft/proposed amendment moving to collective 51% compliance for group captive projects: reported as a government proposal at research time (Mercom India, Law.asia) - confirm whether it has been formally notified as final rules (versus still in draft/consultation) at drafting time

APTEL captive-status denial example (hotel denied captive status for insufficient equity): this is a live case already covered on this site's Legal Updates page - cross-reference rather than re-narrate the case facts

topic_title: How to File an Appeal Before the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT)
angle: A practical guide for a taxpayer who has lost before the Commissioner of Income Tax (Appeals) and wants to appeal to the ITAT - covering the limitation period, the prescribed form, filing fees, and the transition to mandatory e-filing that practitioners report is underway in 2026.
key_points: An appeal to the ITAT against a CIT(A) order lies under Section 253 of the Income Tax Act, 1961

Filing fee is slab-based on the assessed total income: Rs. 500 where assessed income is up to Rs. 1 lakh, Rs. 1,500 where it exceeds Rs. 1 lakh but is up to Rs. 2 lakh, and 1% of assessed income (subject to a Rs. 10,000 cap) above that
ITAT has discretion to condone delay in filing for sufficient cause shown, but the appeal should be filed within the statutory limitation window running from the date the CIT(A) order is communicated

Practitioner sources report a transition to mandatory e-filing with digital signature authentication, and a new prescribed appeal form (reported as Form 115) intended to replace the long-standing Form 36 - treat this as a live procedural change to confirm against the current Income Tax (Appellate Tribunal) Rules before relying on either form
Required enclosures typically include a certified copy of the CIT(A) order, the grounds of appeal, and the fee payment challan, uploaded via the tribunal's e-filing portal

Practical tip: an appeal that is incomplete (wrong form, missing enclosures, or fee shortfall) risks being treated as not properly instituted, so practitioners should confirm the current form number and portal requirements immediately before filing rather than relying on last year's checklist
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: Section 253 as the governing provision for appeals to ITAT: settled, confirmed via Income Tax Act structure and multiple practitioner sources

Slab-based filing fee structure (Rs. 500 / Rs. 1,500 / 1% capped at Rs. 10,000): confirmed via ClearTax and TaxBuddy guides at research time - verify against the current fee schedule under Section 253(6) at drafting time since fee slabs are periodically revised

60-day limitation period from communication of the CIT(A) order: this is the well-established figure under Section 253(3) - one lower-authority source found at research time cited an incorrect section number ('Section 362', which does not exist in the Income Tax Act) for this limitation period, so the exact provision and day-count MUST be verified directly against the current Section 253(3) text before drafting, not taken from that source

Transition from Form 36 to a new Form 115 and mandatory DSC-based e-filing effective 2026: reported by several SEO-oriented tax-filing blogs (ClearTax, TaxBuddy, Patron Accounting) at research time but not yet cross-checked against an official CBDT/ITAT notification - flag as unconfirmed and verify against the official notification before publishing, or hedge the guide to describe the process generically if the new form/rules cannot be confirmed by drafting time

topic_title: Filing Your Claim as a Creditor in a Company's CIRP: Forms and Deadlines
angle: A practical guide for a creditor (financial, operational, or other) who has just learned that a debtor company has entered Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process, walking through which form to use, the filing deadline, what happens if that deadline is missed, and how claims get verified.
key_points: The prescribed claim forms under the CIRP Regulations, 2016 vary by creditor category - Form C is used by financial creditors and Form B by operational creditors (other than workmen/employees), with separate forms (including Forms CA, D, E and F) for other categories such as workmen, employees, and creditors in a class

Under Regulation 12(1), a creditor must submit its claim with supporting proof to the Interim Resolution Professional (IRP) on or before the last date specified in the public announcement - ordinarily the fourteenth day from the IRP's appointment

A creditor who misses that initial window is not automatically shut out: the first proviso to Regulation 12(1) allows a late claim to be filed up to the date the Resolution Professional issues the Form G invitation for resolution plans, or ninety days from the insolvency commencement date, whichever is later

Once received, the Resolution Professional is required to verify claims within 7 days of the last date for receipt under Regulation 13(1), and admits, rejects or seeks further information/clarification on each claim

Practical filing checklist: the claim form itself, documentary proof of debt (invoices, loan/facility agreements, account statements, or a decree/award if the debt is already adjudicated), and, where relevant, evidence of any security interest held

Claims filed late, on the wrong form, or without adequate supporting evidence face a real risk of rejection or only partial admission - creditors should not wait for a personal notice and should instead monitor the public announcement and IBBI/NCLT records proactively once they learn of a CIRP against their debtor
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: Form B (operational creditors) / Form C (financial creditors) and the 14-day claim submission window under Regulation 12(1) of the CIRP Regulations, 2016: well-established and confirmed across IBC Laws, TaxGuru and IBBI's own claim-verification FAQs at research time

First proviso to Regulation 12(1) allowing late claims up to the Form G issuance date or 90 days from insolvency commencement, whichever is later: confirmed via a 2026 practitioner guide at research time - verify the exact regulation text and any 2026 amendment to this proviso against the current CIRP Regulations before drafting
7-day claim verification timeline under Regulation 13(1): confirmed via ICSI IIP knowledge capsule and IBC Laws at research time

topic_title: Registering an Industrial Design in India: Process, Timeline and Protection
angle: A practical guide for a manufacturer or product designer seeking to protect the visual appearance (shape, configuration, pattern or ornamentation) of an article under the Designs Act, 2000 - distinct from the site's existing patent, trademark and copyright registration guides, this fills the remaining major IP registration route not yet covered.
key_points: The Designs Act, 2000 protects only features of shape, configuration, pattern, ornament or composition of lines/colours applied to an article - it does not protect the article's underlying function or any mode/principle of construction (that is the domain of patents)

Applications are filed with the Design Office (headquartered in Kolkata, with filing also accepted at the four patent office branches) and must specify a single Locarno Classification class from India's 32-class system - a design can be registered in one class per application
For an uncontested application, registration typically takes roughly 6-12 months, though timelines vary depending on office objections and responses

Protection initially runs for 10 years from the date of registration, and can be extended for a further 5 years (15 years total) by filing Form-3 with the prescribed renewal fee before the first 10-year term expires

The Design (Amendment) Rules, 2014 created differentiated fee slabs for 'natural person' applicants versus other applicants (companies, etc.), and DPIIT-recognised startups and small entities are eligible for substantially reduced official fees

A design must be new or original and not previously published or used anywhere in India or elsewhere prior to the filing date - unlike trademarks, there is no renewable-forever protection, so timing the filing before any public disclosure or product launch is critical
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: Core Designs Act, 2000 framework (protectable subject matter, exclusion of function/construction principle): settled statutory position, confirmed across multiple practitioner guides (Intepat, LawBhoomi, IP Coster) at research time
32-class Locarno Classification system and one-class-per-application rule: confirmed via multiple sources at research time

10-year initial term + 5-year extension via Form-3: confirmed via multiple sources at research time - verify current renewal fee amount (cited as around Rs. 2,000 in one source) against the current Designs Rules fee schedule at drafting time

Reduced fees for natural persons, startups and small entities under the 2014 Amendment Rules: confirmed generally at research time - verify the current exact fee table (which may have been revised since 2014) against the Designs Rules in force at drafting time

topic_title: Deemed Conveyance: How a Housing Society Gets Land Title When the Builder Won't Convey It
angle: A practical guide for a housing society or flat owners' association whose builder has failed to execute a conveyance deed, explaining the deemed conveyance mechanism under Section 11 of RERA (for RERA-registered projects) and Section 11 of MOFA (for older Maharashtra projects), the application process before the Competent Authority, and how it differs from a voluntary conveyance.
key_points: A promoter is legally obligated to convey title/land to the association of allottees - under RERA, within three months of the occupancy certificate being issued; under Maharashtra's MOFA, within four months of the flat purchasers' organisation being formed

Where the promoter fails or refuses to execute a conveyance deed, allottees/the association need not sue in a civil court - they can apply for a unilateral 'deemed conveyance' before the Competent Authority (in Maharashtra, the District Deputy Registrar of Cooperative Societies), which can register the conveyance without the promoter's participation

The application is made in a prescribed form (Form VII under the MOFA Rules) with the requisite court-fee stamp, enclosing true copies of members' registered agreements for sale, society registration certificate, and other project documents

A deemed conveyance under RERA/MOFA passes title to the land and building to the society, but does NOT by itself resolve outstanding disputes over additional FSI, unauthorised construction, or amenities the builder failed to provide - those typically need to be pursued separately

Recent amendments and case law have addressed the status of deemed conveyance orders passed before statutory changes, and societies should confirm the current procedural rules in their state (the mechanism and its exact procedural details are Maharashtra-specific under MOFA; other states rely primarily on RERA's Section 11 framework, which may be procedurally thinner)

Practical tip: societies should apply for deemed conveyance promptly after formation rather than waiting - delay does not defeat the right, but it does delay the society's ability to raise its own redevelopment, loans, or repairs requiring clear title
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: RERA Section 11 three-month conveyance timeline from occupancy certificate: confirmed via TaxGuru and IBC Laws' summaries of Section 11 at research time

MOFA Section 11 four-month timeline from formation of the flat purchasers' organisation, and the Form VII/Rule 12 deemed conveyance application process with a Rs. 2,000 court-fee stamp: confirmed via Chambers and Partners and Mondaq coverage at research time - this MOFA mechanism is Maharashtra-specific; verify whether the state where the guide will be primarily used has an equivalent state-level deemed-conveyance procedure or relies solely on RERA Section 11 remedies

2025 MOFA amendment and its effect on deemed conveyance orders passed before the amendment (flagged as still valid by Bombay High Court per LiveLawBiz coverage at research time): treat as a live, evolving area and verify the current state of the law before drafting rather than treating pre-amendment orders' validity as settled

Deemed conveyance not resolving separate disputes over additional FSI/unauthorised construction: general practitioner consensus at research time, not tied to a specific statutory provision - present as practical guidance rather than a citation

topic_title: Contract Farming Agreements in India: What Agribusinesses and Farmers Should Get Right
angle: A practical guide for an agribusiness (processor, exporter, or aggregator) or farmer entering a contract farming/produce-purchase arrangement, explaining the current legal landscape after the 2020 central farm laws were repealed in 2021 - what governs these contracts today, what the advisory 2018 Model Act recommends, and the drafting points that matter most given the absence of a uniform national statute.
key_points: The Farmers (Empowerment and Protection) Agreement on Price Assurance and Farm Services Act, 2020 - which had created a specific central legal framework for contract farming - was repealed by Parliament in 2021 along with the other two farm laws, so there is currently no dedicated central contract-farming statute in force

In the absence of that repealed framework, a contract farming arrangement today is governed primarily by ordinary principles of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, together with whatever state-specific APMC Act amendments or standalone contract-farming provisions the relevant state has separately enacted (several states had amended their APMC Acts to permit and register contract farming even before the 2020 central law)

The Ministry of Agriculture's Model Agriculture Produce and Livestock Contract Farming and Services (Promotion & Facilitation) Act, 2018 remains a non-binding template that states may draw on - it recommended registering contracts with a Registering and Agreement Recording Committee, keeping contract farming outside ordinary APMC market-fee obligations, and a tiered local dispute-resolution mechanism (Sub-Divisional Authority and Appellate Authority) - but it has no force of law unless a state has actually adopted it

Because the legal landscape varies significantly by state, businesses should first confirm whether the state(s) where the farming will occur have their own contract-farming registration/dispute-resolution provisions (via APMC Act amendments or separate legislation) before assuming any particular procedure applies

Essential drafting points regardless of jurisdiction: a clear pricing/price-assurance formula (including how quality specifications and grading disputes will be resolved), delivery and quality-acceptance terms, provision for force majeure/crop failure, and an express dispute-resolution clause (arbitration or a named local forum) - since without a dedicated statutory forum, disputes will otherwise default to ordinary civil litigation

Sponsors should also be careful that the agreement does not purport to transfer, encumber, or create any interest in the farmer's land itself - a core protection that was a central point of the repealed 2020 Act and remains good drafting practice regardless of which framework technically governs the state
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: Repeal of the 2020 farm laws (including the Farmers (Empowerment and Protection) Agreement Act) in 2021: settled, well-documented fact

Current absence of a dedicated central contract-farming statute, with the field reverting to the Indian Contract Act plus state APMC frameworks: consistent with PRS India and Wikipedia summaries at research time - verify the specific state(s) the guide will target for any state-level contract farming provisions before drafting, since this varies considerably state to state and should not be generalised as uniform

2018 Model Contract Farming Act's registration, market-fee exemption, and tiered dispute-resolution features: confirmed via PRS India and PIB press releases at research time - it is explicitly a non-binding model/template, not an enacted central law, and this distinction must be preserved in the guide

Recommendation against agreements creating interest in farmer's land: reflects a core protective feature Parliament built into the now-repealed 2020 Act - present as best-practice drafting advice, not as a currently binding statutory requirement

topic_title: How to File a GST Appeal Before the Commissioner (Appeals): Form APL-01, Pre-Deposit and Timelines
angle: A practical guide for a taxpayer who has received an adverse GST demand or order at the first (adjudicating authority) level, explaining the first-appeal route to the Commissioner (Appeals) under Section 107 of the CGST Act - distinct from the GST Appellate Tribunal (GSTAT) guide already covered on the site, which deals with the next stage of appeal.
key_points: An appeal against an order of an adjudicating authority lies to the Commissioner (Appeals) under Section 107(1) of the CGST Act, 2017, filed electronically in FORM GST APL-01 within three months of communication of the order (extendable by one further month on sufficient cause shown)

Mandatory pre-deposit under Section 107(6): the full amount of tax, interest, fine, fee and penalty admitted as due, plus 10% of the remaining disputed tax amount, subject to a cap (verify current cap, reported as Rs. 20 crore at research time, at drafting)
Once the pre-deposit is made and the appeal is admitted, recovery proceedings for the balance disputed amount are automatically stayed

The appeal must be verified and accompanied by a certified copy of the decision/order appealed against and relevant supporting documents; a cross-objection can be filed by the respondent within 45 days

The Commissioner (Appeals) can confirm, modify or annul the order but cannot refer the case back to the adjudicating authority for a fresh decision, and cannot enhance a penalty or fee or demand without giving the appellant a reasonable opportunity of being heard
A further appeal from the Commissioner (Appeals)'s order lies to the GST Appellate Tribunal (GSTAT) - the next stage, already covered in a separate guide on this site
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: Three-month filing window (extendable by one month) and FORM GST APL-01 as the prescribed form: well-settled under Section 107 CGST Act, confirmed via ClearTax, GST portal user manual and Vakilsearch guides at research time

10% pre-deposit of disputed tax with a monetary cap, and the April 2026 GST portal fix making the pre-deposit percentage field editable: confirmed via multiple 2026 sources at research time - verify the current cap amount and any further portal changes at drafting time
Commissioner (Appeals) barred from remanding the matter back to the adjudicating authority: confirmed under the proviso to Section 107(11) of the CGST Act

topic_title: Applying for a Mining Lease in India: The Process Under the MMDR Act
angle: A practical guide for a business seeking to mine minerals in India, walking through the application process to the state government under the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957 and the Mineral Concession Rules - covering major vs minor minerals, the auction-based grant regime for major minerals, and the compliance obligations (mining plan, DMF, environmental/forest clearances) that follow grant.
key_points: Mining of 'major minerals' is governed by the MMDR Act, 1957 (as substantially amended in 2015 and thereafter) and is granted primarily through competitive auction by the state government, while 'minor minerals' are regulated by state governments under their own rules

An application for a mining lease over notified/auctioned blocks proceeds through the state government's e-auction process; areas not yet auctioned may in limited circumstances still involve applications in the prescribed Form under the Mineral Concession Rules, 1960

Grant of lease requires the area to have been prospected and reserves established, an approved Mining Plan (and Mine Closure Plan) sanctioned by the Indian Bureau of Mines or state authority, and, for coal/lignite, prior Central Government approval
A mining lessee must contribute to the District Mineral Foundation (DMF) and the National Mineral Exploration Trust (NMET) as prescribed under the Act and Rules

Environmental Clearance (under the EIA Notification, 2006) and, where forest land is involved, Forest Clearance under the Forest (Conservation) Act are separate, mandatory pre-conditions before mining operations can commence, in addition to the lease itself

Maximum lease period and renewal norms, and state-specific procedural variations (especially for minor minerals), should be checked against the applicable state's mineral concession rules at drafting time
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: Auction-based grant regime for major minerals introduced by the 2015 MMDR Amendment: well-settled, confirmed via Ministry of Mines and PRS Legislative Research sources at research time
DMF and NMET contribution obligations under Rule 9B of the MMDR framework: confirmed at research time

Central Government approval requirement for coal/lignite leases: confirmed via Ministry of Mines sources - verify current lease tenure figures and any 2026 amendments to the MMDR Act/Rules at drafting time, since this area has seen frequent legislative change

topic_title: Registering a Geographical Indication (GI) in India: Process, Eligibility and Who Can Apply
angle: A practical guide for a producer association, farmers' collective, or state agency seeking to protect a regional product (agricultural, food, handicraft or industrial) under the Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999 - distinct from the site's existing trademark/patent/copyright/industrial-design guides.
key_points: Only an association of persons, producers, or an organisation/authority representing the interests of producers of the goods (not an individual trader in most cases) can apply for GI registration, by filing Form GI-1A to GI-1D (as applicable) with the Geographical Indications Registry in Chennai

The application must be filed in triplicate with a statement of how the goods' quality, reputation or characteristics are essentially attributable to their geographical origin, supported by maps, production process details and a list of producers

Government fee is charged per class (reported as Rs. 5,000 for individuals/associations, Rs. 10,000 for government/other applicants at research time - verify current GI Rules, 2002 fee schedule at drafting), and the process includes examination, a two-month window to respond to objections, advertisement in the GI Journal, and (if unopposed or after opposition is resolved) entry in the GI Register
The full registration process typically takes many months to a couple of years depending on objections and the examiner's queries
A registered GI is valid for 10 years from the date of registration and can be renewed indefinitely for further 10-year periods on payment of the renewal fee

Registration confers the right to exclude others from using the GI on goods not originating in the defined region, and authorised users (registered separately from the GI itself) can use the GI logo/tag; unauthorised use can attract infringement action
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: Applicant eligibility restricted to associations/producer bodies rather than individuals: confirmed under Section 11 of the GI Act, 1999 at research time

Forms GI-1A-GI-1D, Chennai registry, two-month objection response window, 10-year validity and renewal: confirmed via IP India's official registration-process page and S.S. Rana & Co. fee schedule at research time - verify current fee amounts against the GI Rules, 2002 (as amended) at drafting time
Typical processing timeline (12-24 months) is an approximation from practitioner sources, not a statutory deadline - present as indicative only

topic_title: Related Party Transactions Under Section 188: When Your Company Needs Board or Shareholder Approval
angle: A practical compliance guide for company directors and CFOs on identifying a 'related party transaction' under Section 188 of the Companies Act, 2013, and navigating the board- and shareholder-approval thresholds - a distinct governance/compliance topic not covered by the site's existing Section 447 (director fraud liability) or NCLT oppression-and-mismanagement guides.
key_points: Section 188 covers specified transactions (sale/purchase of goods or property, leasing of property, availing/rendering of services, appointment of agents, and certain appointments to office or place of profit) between a company and its 'related parties' as defined in Section 2(76)

All covered related-party transactions require prior Board approval by resolution passed at a duly convened Board meeting - approval by circular resolution is not permitted, and an interested director must not be present or vote on that agenda item

Beyond Board approval, transactions exceeding the materiality thresholds prescribed under Rule 15 of the Companies (Meetings of Board and its Powers) Rules, 2014 (e.g., a percentage of annual turnover or net worth for sale/purchase of goods, property, leasing, etc.) additionally require prior approval of shareholders by an ordinary or special resolution, with related-party shareholders barred from voting on the resolution

For listed companies, SEBI's LODR Regulations impose materiality thresholds and audit-committee approval requirements for related-party transactions that are separate from, and often stricter than, the Companies Act thresholds

A contract or arrangement entered into without the required Board or shareholder approval is voidable at the Board's option, and any director or employee who authorised it may be required to indemnify the company for any resulting loss and can face a penalty

Certain transactions in the 'ordinary course of business' and made on an 'arm's length basis' are exempt from the shareholder-approval requirement, though not from disclosure and Board-approval obligations - correctly characterising a transaction as arm's length/ordinary course is often the crux of practical disputes
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: Section 188 scope, mandatory Board approval with interested-director recusal, and voidability for non-compliance: well-settled, confirmed via iPleaders, TaxGuru and CAIRR commentary at research time

Rule 15 materiality thresholds triggering shareholder approval: confirmed at research time - verify exact current percentage/turnover figures against the Companies (Meetings of Board and its Powers) Rules, 2014 (as amended) at drafting time, since these thresholds have been revised before
Penalty range (reported as Rs. 25,000 to Rs. 5,00,000) should be re-verified against the current Section 188 penalty provision at drafting time

topic_title: Retrenching an Employee in India: Notice, Compensation and Process Under the Industrial Relations Code
angle: A practical guide for an employer needing to retrench workers (as distinct from disciplinary termination or resignation), explaining the notice and compensation requirements that were under Section 25F of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 and now sit in the Industrial Relations Code, 2020 following the four Labour Codes coming into force on 21 November 2025 - a distinct, process-focused companion to the site's existing broad 'India's New Labour Codes' overview article.
key_points: 'Retrenchment' is termination of a workman's service for reasons other than disciplinary punishment (e.g., surplus staff, business reasons) - it does not cover voluntary resignation, retirement, or non-renewal of a fixed-term contract on expiry

A workman in continuous service for not less than one year cannot be retrenched until given one month's written notice (or wages in lieu), payment of retrenchment compensation equal to 15 days' average pay for every completed year of continuous service (or part exceeding six months), and notice to the appropriate Government in the prescribed manner

References to the old Section 25F of the Industrial Disputes Act are now to be read as the corresponding provision of the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, which came into force along with the other three Labour Codes on 21 November 2025

For industrial establishments employing 300 or more workers (a threshold raised from the earlier 100-worker cap under the old law), prior permission of the appropriate Government is additionally required before retrenchment, layoff or closure under the Code's Chapter on special provisions

'Last come, first go' (retrenching the most recently hired workman in a category first) is the general principle employers are expected to follow absent a contrary agreement, though it is not an absolute rule in all circumstances

A retrenched workman has re-employment preference if the employer proposes to take on workers again within a prescribed period, and failure to follow the mandatory notice/compensation/permission requirements can expose the employer to reinstatement and back-wages claims
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: Section 25F requirements (one month notice/wages in lieu, 15 days' average pay per completed year, government notice) carried forward into the Industrial Relations Code, 2020: confirmed via multiple 2026 practitioner sources at research time

300-worker threshold for the prior-permission requirement under the new Code (up from 100 under the old Industrial Disputes Act): commonly reported figure - verify the exact current threshold and whether any state-specific variation applies at drafting time, since states have historically set differing thresholds via amendment
21 November 2025 commencement date for the four Labour Codes: confirmed, consistent with the site's existing labour-codes coverage

topic_title: How Banks Classify a Loan as an NPA — and How Borrowers Can Challenge a Wrongful Classification
angle: A practical guide for a borrower whose account has been tagged as a Non-Performing Asset, explaining RBI's 90-day IRAC classification rule, the procedural safeguards a bank must follow, and the legal remedies available before and after a SARFAESI notice - a distinct topic from the site's existing SARFAESI Section 13(2) response guide, focused on contesting the NPA tag itself rather than responding to enforcement.
key_points: Under RBI's Prudential Norms on Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning (IRACP), an account is classified as an NPA when interest or principal remains overdue for more than 90 days, with classification treated as valid once made on or after the 90th day of continuing irregularity

RBI's fair practices expectations require banks to follow their Board-approved recovery policy, including adequate notice/intimation to the borrower, before and around NPA classification - though classification itself is a prudential/accounting determination, not a quasi-judicial order requiring a personal hearing at that stage

A borrower who believes classification was premature or procedurally flawed (e.g., the 90-day overdue period was wrongly computed, or payments were misapplied) can raise this directly with the bank's grievance/nodal officer and, if unresolved, escalate to the Banking Ombudsman under the RBI Integrated Ombudsman Scheme

Once a Section 13(2) SARFAESI demand notice follows an NPA classification, a borrower who disputes the classification or the measures taken under Section 13(4) can file a Securitisation Application under Section 17 of the SARFAESI Act before the Debts Recovery Tribunal

Courts have upheld classification made strictly on the 90th day of continuing default as lawful and not 'premature', so a challenge succeeds only by showing an actual computational, procedural or documentary error - not by disputing the 90-day rule itself

Distinguish NPA classification (an internal prudential tag with credit-reporting consequences) from 'wilful defaulter' classification and from SARFAESI enforcement action - each carries different consequences and different procedural safeguards
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: 90-day overdue threshold under RBI's IRACP Master Circular/Directions: well-settled and confirmed at research time

Judicial recognition that classification on the exact 90th day is valid and not premature: confirmed via a 2025-26 Delhi High Court ruling (Canara Bank v. M/s Krishna Enterprises) reported by Verdictum and Taxscan at research time - verify exact citation at drafting time
Section 17 SARFAESI Act as the remedy once enforcement measures follow: well-settled

Banking Ombudsman/RBI Integrated Ombudsman Scheme as a grievance-escalation route for classification disputes prior to SARFAESI action: general regulatory framework, confirmed at research time - verify current scheme name/coverage at drafting time

topic_title: Challenging an Arbitral Award Under Section 34: Grounds, Timeline and Procedure
angle: A practical guide for an award-debtor considering whether and how to challenge a domestic arbitral award in an Indian court, distinct from the site's existing foreign-award enforcement guide - covering the narrow statutory grounds, the strict limitation window, and what a Section 34 court will and will not re-examine.
key_points: An application to set aside a domestic award is filed under Section 34 before the court with jurisdiction (as defined by Section 2(1)(e) and, for Commercial Courts Act-notified value thresholds, the relevant Commercial Court/Division)

Strict limitation: the application must be made within three months from the date the applicant received the arbitral award (or, where applicable, from disposal of a Section 33 correction/interpretation request), extendable by a further 30 days only on sufficient cause shown - and courts have held this outer limit of three months plus 30 days cannot be extended further even under Section 5 of the Limitation Act

Limited grounds under Section 34(2): party incapacity, invalid arbitration agreement, lack of proper notice or inability to present one's case, award dealing with matters beyond the scope of submission, improper composition of the tribunal or procedure, and - on the court's own examination - subject-matter not arbitrable or the award being in conflict with the public policy of India

For purely domestic awards only (not international commercial arbitrations seated in India), 'patent illegality appearing on the face of the award' is an additional ground, but the proviso expressly bars setting aside merely for an erroneous application of law or by reappreciating evidence
A Section 34 court does not sit in appeal over the arbitral tribunal's findings of fact or its interpretation of the contract - the scrutiny is supervisory and narrow, not a fresh look at the merits

Filing a Section 34 application does not automatically stay enforcement of the award; a separate stay application must be made and, per the 2015/2021 amendments, an unconditional stay generally requires the court to be satisfied a prima facie case exists that the underlying arbitration agreement or contract was induced by fraud or corruption
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: Three-month limitation plus 30-day condonable extension, with an absolute outer limit: well-settled under Section 34(3) and confirmed via Mondaq, iPleaders and Singhania & Co. commentary at research time
Section 34(2) grounds and the domestic-only patent-illegality ground with its proviso: well-settled, confirmed at research time

Automatic-stay vs conditional-stay position after the 2015/2021 amendments to Section 36: confirm the current text against the latest amendment at drafting time, since this provision has been amended more than once

topic_title: Invoking (or Resisting) a Bank Guarantee: The Fraud and Special-Equities Exceptions
angle: A practical guide for a beneficiary seeking to invoke an unconditional bank guarantee, and for an applicant/bank seeking to resist encashment - explaining why Indian courts almost always refuse to interfere, and the two narrow exceptions where an injunction can succeed.
key_points: A bank guarantee is treated as an independent contract between the bank and the beneficiary, separate from the underlying commercial contract between the beneficiary and the applicant - a mere dispute under the underlying contract is not a ground to restrain invocation

Where the guarantee is unconditional and its terms are met (a written demand in the specified form, within its validity period), the bank is bound to honour it regardless of disputes between the beneficiary and the applicant

Courts will grant an injunction against invocation only in two narrow, well-recognised exceptions: (i) 'egregious fraud' of a kind that vitiates the entire underlying transaction and of which the bank had notice, established through clear, contemporaneous documentary evidence - not merely alleged; or (ii) 'special equities' where honouring the guarantee would cause irretrievable injustice that cannot later be compensated by damages

Merely using the word 'fraud' in pleadings, or pointing to an ongoing dispute over the underlying contract's performance, is insufficient - the fraud must be of the guarantee transaction itself, not just the underlying commercial relationship
An applicant seeking an injunction must move quickly and with strong contemporaneous evidence; courts have progressively sharpened the evidentiary threshold for both exceptions in recent rulings

A beneficiary invoking a guarantee should ensure its demand strictly complies with the guarantee's own conditions (form, timing, authorised signatory) since technical non-compliance is one of the few grounds on which invocation itself (as opposed to encashment) can be challenged
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: Independent-contract principle and the general bar on injunctions absent fraud/special equities: well-settled Supreme Court position, confirmed via Conventus Law, SCC Online Blog and Cyril Amarchand Mangaldas commentary at research time

The two exceptions (egregious fraud vitiating the transaction; special equities/irretrievable injustice) and their high evidentiary bar: confirmed at research time - note a February 2026 Delhi High Court ruling reported as sharpening these thresholds further; verify and cite that specific ruling at drafting time
Do not name a specific limitation period for challenging invocation, since none was confirmed at research time - present the guidance as 'act promptly' rather than citing a fixed number of days

topic_title: Getting a Temporary Injunction: What You Must Show Under Order XXXIX Rules 1 and 2 CPC
angle: A practical guide for a plaintiff seeking urgent interim relief in a civil or commercial suit, and for a defendant resisting one - walking through the three-part test courts apply and how each element is actually proved in practice, as a companion to the site's existing commercial-litigation and arbitration-clause guides.
key_points: Order XXXIX Rule 1 empowers a court to restrain a threatened breach or injury before trial; Rule 2 covers injunctions to restrain a continuing or repeated breach of contract or other injury, both 'when it is just and convenient to do so'

The Supreme Court (Dalpat Kumar v. Prahlad Singh and subsequent rulings) requires the applicant to satisfy three elements cumulatively: a prima facie case, balance of convenience in the applicant's favour, and irreparable injury that cannot be adequately compensated in damages
Prima facie case is a threshold requirement, not proof of eventual success - but if it is not met, the court will not go on to weigh balance of convenience or irreparable harm at all

Irreparable injury does not mean the harm must be literally irreversible - it means the injury is of a kind that money alone cannot fairly compensate (e.g., loss of a unique property interest, breach of a negative covenant, or reputational harm)

Balance of convenience requires comparing the hardship to the applicant if relief is refused against the hardship to the opposite party if relief is granted; courts also weigh public interest where relevant

An ex parte ad interim injunction (granted without hearing the opposite side) is meant to be a short, urgent stop-gap measure — the court must record reasons for granting it ex parte, and the defendant is entitled to apply promptly for its vacation once served
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: Three-part cumulative test (prima facie case, balance of convenience, irreparable injury) from Dalpat Kumar v. Prahlad Singh: well-settled Supreme Court precedent, confirmed via multiple practitioner sources at research time
Requirement to record reasons for an ex parte injunction under Order XXXIX Rule 3 CPC: well-settled statutory requirement
General procedural framework (application, affidavit, notice to opposite party except in urgent cases): confirmed at research time

topic_title: Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020: What Online Sellers and Marketplaces Must Disclose
angle: A compliance guide for an e-commerce marketplace entity or an inventory-based/individual seller operating in India, explaining the specific disclosure, fair-trade-practice and grievance-redressal obligations under the 2020 Rules - a distinct, e-commerce-specific companion to the site's general consumer-complaint-filing guide.
key_points: The Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020 apply to all forms of e-commerce, including marketplace and inventory-based models, and to every seller offering goods or services through such platforms, whether or not the seller is based in India

Marketplace e-commerce entities must display, for every seller on the platform, details such as legal name, principal geographic address, customer care contact details, GSTIN (where applicable), and a ranking/search-result policy that does not discriminate against sellers arbitrarily

Sellers must furnish the marketplace with accurate information on return, refund, exchange, warranty/guarantee, delivery and shipment timelines, and mode of payment, so consumers can make an informed pre-purchase decision, and must not falsely represent themselves as a different seller or as a 'consumer' posting a review

Both marketplace entities and sellers are barred from unfair trade practices, including manipulating price to gain unreasonable profit and refusing return/refund/exchange for defective, deficient, spurious, or materially different goods (subject to a genuine force-majeure exception for delivery delays)

Every e-commerce entity must appoint a grievance officer and display their name and contact details, and must acknowledge a consumer complaint within 48 hours and redress it within one month from the date of receipt

Marketplace entities are required to verify sellers' business details (address, GST registration where applicable) before onboarding them, and must not manipulate search results/rankings to favour their own related-party sellers over unrelated ones
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: Rules' effective date (23 July 2020), scope covering both marketplace and inventory models, and seller/marketplace disclosure obligations: well-settled, confirmed via Trilegal, Lexology and official consumerprotection.in sources at research time

48-hour acknowledgment and one-month redressal timeline for grievance officers: confirmed at research time - re-verify against the current Rules (as they have seen proposed amendments) at drafting time

Note that amendments to these Rules have been proposed/discussed since 2021 - confirm whether any amendment has actually been notified and is in force as of drafting time, rather than assuming the 2020 text is unchanged

topic_title: Private Placement of Shares Under Section 42: Process, PAS-4 and Compliance Timelines
angle: A practical compliance guide for a private company raising capital from a select group of investors without a public offer, distinct from the site's existing Section 188 (related-party transactions) and M&A due-diligence guides - covering the shareholder approval, offer-letter, allotment and filing mechanics.
key_points: Private placement under Section 42 of the Companies Act, 2013 means offering securities to a select, identified group rather than to the public, and requires a prior Special Resolution of shareholders approving the specific offer or invitation before the offer letter is issued

The offer can be made to not more than 200 persons in aggregate per class of security in a financial year (excluding qualified institutional buyers and employees under an ESOP scheme), per Rule 14 of the Companies (Prospectus and Allotment of Securities) Rules, 2014 - exceeding this deems the offer a public issue attracting prospectus requirements

The private placement offer letter (Form PAS-4) must be issued only to the identified persons, cannot be circulated publicly or through any media/marketing/agent, and application money must be received only through banking channels, not cash

Securities must be allotted within 60 days of receipt of application money; if not allotted within that period, the company must refund the money within 15 days of expiry, failing which it attracts interest at 12% per annum from the 60th day

The company must file the return of allotment (Form PAS-3) with the Registrar within 15 days of allotment, and separately file the private placement offer letter details with the Registrar within 30 days of circulating it, along with the complete list of offerees

A company cannot make a fresh private placement offer of the same kind of security until the earlier allotment is completed, withdrawn or the offer lapses, and penalties (company and every officer in default, plus refund of monies with interest) apply for non-compliance with Section 42's conditions
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: Special resolution requirement, 200-person cap under Rule 14, and PAS-4/PAS-3 forms: well-settled, confirmed via iPleaders, ClearTax and Marg ERP commentary at research time
60-day allotment deadline and 15-day refund-with-12%-interest consequence: confirmed at research time

30-day Registrar filing deadline for the offer letter: confirmed at research time - re-verify exact day-counts against the current Companies (Prospectus and Allotment of Securities) Rules, 2014 (as amended) at drafting time, since these figures have been subject to amendment

topic_title: Fixed-Term Employment Contracts in India: Rights, Parity and When They End
angle: A practical guide for an employer considering fixed-term hiring and for an employee on a fixed-term contract, explaining what fixed-term employment is under the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) framework and the Industrial Relations Code, the parity guarantees fixed-term workers enjoy, and what happens when the term expires.
key_points: Fixed-term employment was formally introduced via the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Central (Amendment) Rules, 2018 (effective 16 March 2018), and later carried forward into the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, giving employers a lawful route to hire for a defined period without treating the worker as 'contract labour' routed through a contractor

A fixed-term worker must get parity with a permanent worker doing the same or similar work in terms of working hours, wages, allowances and other statutory benefits, proportionate to the length of service actually rendered

Notably, a fixed-term worker becomes eligible for statutory benefits like gratuity on a proportionate basis even if their contract period is shorter than the qualifying period ordinarily required (e.g., the usual five-year continuous-service threshold for gratuity) - this is a key point of difference from ordinary fixed-term or contract engagements

Non-renewal or natural expiry of a fixed-term contract at the end of its stated term is not treated as 'retrenchment' and does not attract the notice/compensation requirements that apply to retrenchment of a permanent workman - but genuine fixed-term status (not a sham used to defeat permanency claims) is essential to this position
The law is prospective and does not permit an employer to convert existing permanent workmen's posts into fixed-term positions to dodge existing protections

Employers should ensure the fixed-term contract genuinely reflects a defined-duration need (project, seasonal demand, etc.) and is properly documented, since courts scrutinise whether repeated renewals or a de facto permanent role disguise what is really a permanent employment relationship
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: 2018 Standing Orders amendment introducing fixed-term employment, and its parity/proportionate-benefits requirements: well-settled, confirmed via Majmudar & Partners and ResearchGate sources at research time

Proportionate gratuity eligibility even below the standard qualifying period for fixed-term workers: confirmed via the 2018 Rules at research time - verify this is preserved without change under the Industrial Relations Code, 2020 as now in force, at drafting time

Non-renewal not constituting retrenchment: general position confirmed at research time, but note courts examine genuineness of the fixed-term arrangement case by case - present this as the general rule with that caveat, not as an absolute

topic_title: FSSAI Food Recall Procedure: What a Food Business Operator Must Do When a Product Is Unsafe
angle: A practical compliance guide for a manufacturer, importer or wholesale distributor of food products on what triggers a mandatory recall, the recall-plan and notification obligations, and coordination with FSSAI - a distinct operational-compliance topic from the site's existing FSSAI licensing-overhaul guide.
key_points: Every food business operator engaged in manufacture, import or wholesale supply of food (not retailers) must maintain an up-to-date, written food recall plan as part of its compliance obligations under the Food Safety and Standards (Food Recall Procedure) Regulations

The FBO's own obligation to act is triggered by its own belief/knowledge that a food it has manufactured, processed, distributed or imported does not comply with food safety requirements - it must immediately initiate recall procedures from the point the food left that FBO's immediate control, and inform the competent authority (the Food Safety Commissioner/Designated Officer)
Recalls are classified by hazard severity, which determines the urgency and depth of the recall required and the information FSSAI expects in the recall report

The recall plan should identify the recall coordinator/team, traceability records (batch/lot numbers, distribution records) enabling the FBO to identify exactly which units are affected and where they were distributed, the method of communicating the recall (to distributors, retailers and, where relevant, the public), and disposal/corrective-action procedures for recalled stock

FSSAI maintains oversight and can itself direct or monitor a recall through the Food Safety Commissioner/Designated Officer, in addition to the FBO's own obligation to self-initiate a recall on becoming aware of non-compliant food

Failure to recall unsafe food promptly can expose the FBO to enforcement action and penalties under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 quite apart from any recall-specific consequences, since supplying unsafe food is itself an offence under the Act
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: Recall-plan obligation applying to manufacturers/importers/wholesale suppliers but not retailers: confirmed via FSSAI's own sample recall-plan guidance document at research time
Self-triggering obligation on the FBO's own belief of non-compliance, with immediate notification to the competent authority: confirmed via the FSSAI Recall Procedure regulation text at research time

Two-class (or more) hazard-severity classification system: general framework confirmed, but the precise number and definition of classes should be verified against the current FSSAI Food Recall Procedure Regulations at drafting time, since sources at research time referenced both a 2011 circular and a later 2017 regulation and were not fully consistent on the classification count

topic_title: Initiating CIRP as an Operational Creditor: The Section 8 Demand Notice and Section 9 Application
angle: A practical guide for an unpaid operational creditor (a supplier, service provider or employee-dues claimant) on how to actually start insolvency proceedings against a defaulting corporate debtor - the initiation stage, distinct from the site's existing guide on filing a claim once someone else's CIRP is already underway.
key_points: An operational creditor may, on occurrence of default, deliver a demand notice of unpaid operational debt (Form 3) or a copy of an invoice demanding payment (Form 4) to the corporate debtor under Section 8 of the IBC, under Rule 5 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy (Application to Adjudicating Authority) Rules, 2016

The corporate debtor has 10 days from delivery of the Section 8 notice to either pay the debt or bring to the operational creditor's notice the existence of a pre-existing dispute (with proof) or the record of a pending suit/arbitration

If no payment is received and no notice of dispute is raised within that 10-day window, the operational creditor can file an application before the NCLT in Form 5 under Section 9, along with a copy of the demand notice/invoice, an affidavit that no notice of dispute has been received, and proof of non-payment such as bank certificates or an information utility record

The minimum threshold default amount for initiating CIRP is Rs. 1 crore (raised from Rs. 1 lakh by Central Government notification dated 24 March 2020) - a default below this threshold cannot found a Section 9 application

The NCLT's inquiry at the admission stage under Section 9 is narrow: it examines only whether a 'plausible' pre-existing dispute genuinely exists (not spurious, hypothetical or illusory) - it does not adjudicate the merits of any contractual or factual dispute, which is reserved for the appropriate civil/contractual forum

A Section 8 demand notice by itself does not extend the limitation period for filing the Section 9 application - the underlying debt claim must still be within its own limitation period (generally three years under the Limitation Act) when the Section 9 application is filed
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: Section 8/9 mechanics, Form 3/4/5, and the 10-day dispute-notice window: well-settled statutory framework confirmed via IBC Laws and CAclubindia commentary at research time
Rs. 1 crore minimum threshold (Notification No. S.O. 1205(E) dated 24 March 2020): confirmed at research time

Narrow 'plausible pre-existing dispute' test at admission and no limitation-extension from a Section 8 notice alone: well-settled Supreme Court position (Mobilox Innovations), confirmed at research time - verify no further legislative change to the threshold or procedure via any 2026 IBC amendment at drafting time

topic_title: Getting Your Trademark Declared 'Well-Known' in India: The Rule 124 Process
angle: A practical guide for a brand owner seeking formal well-known-mark status directly from the Trade Marks Registry (rather than waiting to establish it defensively in opposition, rectification or infringement litigation) - covering the Form TM-M application, evidentiary requirements, and what the designation is actually worth.
key_points: Rule 124 of the Trade Marks Rules, 2017 created a standalone administrative procedure allowing a proprietor to apply directly to the Registrar for determination of their mark as 'well-known', without needing to wait for an opposition, rectification or infringement proceeding to raise the question

The application is filed in Form TM-M with the prescribed fee (per the First Schedule to the Rules), accompanied by a detailed statement of case and evidence addressing the Section 11(6)-(9) factors - such as the extent of knowledge/recognition of the mark among the relevant public, duration and geographical extent of use and promotion, and any successful enforcement history recognising the mark as well-known
Before determining the mark as well-known, the Registrar may invite objections from the public/interested parties, to be filed within 30 days of the invitation being published

If the Registrar determines the mark as well-known, it is published in the Trade Marks Journal and added to the official list of well-known trademarks maintained by the Registry - a status that gives cross-class protection (blocking confusingly similar marks even on unrelated goods/services) under Section 11(2)

A formal Rule 124 declaration is not the only route to well-known status - a court can still recognise a mark as well-known during litigation even without a prior Rule 124 declaration, and (per recent Delhi High Court case law) a formal declaration is not even a mandatory precondition to invoking Section 11(2) protection with sufficient reputation evidence

Because the criteria and evidentiary bar are demanding and success is not guaranteed, brand owners should assemble strong, India-specific evidence of recognition (sales figures, advertising spend, media coverage, prior enforcement successes) before filing, rather than relying on global reputation alone
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: Rule 124 procedure, Form TM-M, and 30-day public objection window: well-settled, confirmed via Mondaq and SpicyIP commentary at research time
Cross-class protection consequence under Section 11(2) once well-known status is granted: well-settled

Formal Rule 124 declaration not being a mandatory precondition to invoking Section 11(2) in litigation: confirmed via 2026 Delhi High Court case law referenced elsewhere in this queue (Zara v. Zora) at research time - cross-check consistency with that item when drafting
Exact fee amount under the First Schedule was not confirmed at research time - verify current fee against the official IP India fee schedule at drafting time

topic_title: Open Access for Power Procurement: Eligibility, Charges and How Industrial Consumers Switch Suppliers
angle: A practical guide for an industrial or commercial electricity consumer considering open access to buy power from a source other than their local discom (including renewable/green power), explaining eligibility thresholds, the charge stack, and how captive structures avoid certain surcharges - a distinct topic from the site's existing captive-power-plant compliance guide, focused on the open access route generally.
key_points: Open access lets an eligible consumer procure electricity directly from a generator or through a trader/exchange instead of, or alongside, their area distribution licensee, using the licensee's or a common carrier's wires on payment of prescribed charges, under Section 42 of the Electricity Act, 2003

Under the Green Energy Open Access Rules, the eligibility threshold for open access specifically for green/renewable power has been reduced to 100 kW (from the general 1 MW threshold that applies to conventional open access), opening the route to smaller commercial and industrial consumers

The charge stack for third-party open access (buying from an unrelated generator) typically includes transmission/wheeling charges, cross-subsidy surcharge (CSS), additional surcharge (AS), and banking/standby charges - each determined by the relevant State Electricity Regulatory Commission

Cross-subsidy surcharge, mandated under Section 42(2) of the Electricity Act, compensates the discom for the subsidy revenue it loses when a high-tariff consumer moves off its network to open access; the Green Energy Open Access Rules cap increases in CSS and remove the additional surcharge for green power to incentivise renewable procurement

A 'captive' structure - where the consumer(s) hold at least 26% equity in the generating plant and consume at least 51% of its output - is treated differently: captive open access is exempt from both cross-subsidy surcharge and additional surcharge, making it materially cheaper than third-party open access

State Electricity Regulatory Commissions determine and periodically revise wheeling charges and surcharges for their state, so the actual landed cost of open-access power varies significantly by state and must be checked against the current state regulations before committing to a switch
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: 100 kW threshold for green energy open access (down from 1 MW general threshold): confirmed via PIB and industry sources on the Green Energy Open Access Rules at research time
26% equity / 51% consumption captive-status threshold and its CSS/AS exemption: well-settled under the Electricity Rules, confirmed at research time

Charge stack composition (wheeling, CSS, AS, banking/standby): confirmed at research time - note that exact rates are state-specific and change periodically via SERC orders, so present rates as illustrative/state-dependent rather than fixed figures

topic_title: Pre-Litigation Mediation in India: The Mediation Act, 2023 and Section 12A of the Commercial Courts Act
angle: A practical guide for a prospective commercial plaintiff (or a party served with a mediation notice) explaining when pre-litigation mediation is mandatory before filing suit, how the process actually runs, what happens if a party skips it, and how a settlement reached in mediation is enforced.
key_points: The Mediation Act, 2023 (Act No. 32 of 2023) creates a unified, staged framework for mediation in India, brought into force progressively from September 2023 onward, but pre-institution mediation for commercial disputes of 'specified value' continues to be governed specifically by Section 12A of the Commercial Courts Act, 2015, now read alongside the Mediation Act's enforcement provisions

Section 12A applies to commercial suits above the 'specified value' threshold (Rs. 3 lakh) and requires a plaintiff who is not seeking any urgent interim relief to first attempt mediation through the prescribed authority before instituting the suit

The Supreme Court's ruling in Patil Automation v. Rakheja Engineers (2022) held Section 12A mandatory, not directory — a suit filed without first exhausting pre-institution mediation, where no urgent interim relief is genuinely sought, is liable to be rejected under Order VII Rule 11 CPC

A plaintiff who does seek urgent interim relief can bypass pre-institution mediation, but courts scrutinise whether the urgency plea is genuine or merely a device to dodge Section 12A — a colourable claim for interim relief will not save the suit

The mediation process itself must ordinarily be completed within three months from the date of the application, extendable by a further two months with the parties' consent, before the plaintiff is free to institute the suit if mediation fails

A settlement reached in mediation must be reduced to writing and signed by the parties and the mediator; once so recorded, it carries the same status and effect as an arbitral award on agreed terms under Section 30(4) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, making it directly enforceable as a decree rather than merely a private contract
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: Mediation Act, 2023 (Act No. 32 of 2023) and its staged commencement from September 2023: confirmed via Wikipedia and multiple practitioner sources at research time
